props.title: Libeled Lady
props.initialSlug: Screwball comedy of deception to thwart lawsuit

sections.content: Libeled Lady (1936) stands as one of the greatest screwball comedies of Hollywood's Golden Age, featuring an all-star quartet of William Powell, Myrna Loy, Jean Harlow, and Spencer Tracy. The film's razor-sharp dialogue and intricate plot machinations showcase MGM at its sophisticated peak. Like My Man Godfrey (1936) and The Awful Truth (1937), it perfectly captures the era's signature blend of romantic farce, class commentary, and rapid-fire wit. The chemistry between Powell and Loy, in their fifth pairing after The Thin Man (1934), crackles with their trademark sophistication.

sections.content: The film's plot - involving a newspaper trying to avoid a libel suit through an elaborate scheme - exemplifies the era's love of mistaken identities and romantic deception. Director Jack Conway, though less celebrated than contemporaries like Howard Hawks or George Cukor, delivers perfectly-timed comedy sequences, especially the fishing scene between Powell and Loy. The film shares DNA with other great newspaper comedies like His Girl Friday (1940) and Nothing Sacred (1937), mixing media satire with romantic entanglements.

What sets Libeled Lady apart is its quadrangle romance structure, rare even for screwball comedies. While films like The Philadelphia Story (1940) and Design for Living (1933) played with multiple romantic leads, few balanced four major stars so effectively. Jean Harlow, in one of her final roles before her untimely death, brings both comedy and pathos to what could have been a thankless role. SUBHEAD: The Golden Age of Screwball Comedy

sections.content: Libeled Lady emerged during the peak years of screwball comedy, alongside classics like Twentieth Century (1934) and Easy Living (1937). The genre flourished under the Production Code, using wit and innuendo to bypass censorship. The film's sophisticated handling of marriage, divorce, and romantic complications demonstrates how clever writing could navigate restrictive guidelines while delivering sharp social commentary.
